read.sections.0.heading.back: Spending now and saving for later
read.sections.0.heading.source: Spending now and saving for later

read.sections.0.text.back: Some choices only affect today, but there are other choices that affect what we can do later. Spending means using money or other resources to get something now, such as food or bus fare. Spending is not a bad thing, because everyone needs some things now. Saving means setting aside part of your money or resources for use later. Saving is indeed hard when we do not have much, but small amounts can, over time, add up to a lot. Sami puts a few coins into a tin at home until he has enough money to buy a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save money together in a group. Each person puts a little money into the group every week, and every week one of them takes all of it.
read.sections.0.text.source: Some choices affect only today, but others affect what we can do later. To spend means to use money or another resource to get something now, such as food or a bus ride. Spending is not bad, because everyone needs some things now. To save means to keep some money or resources for later. Saving is hard when there is not much, but small amounts can add up over time. Sami puts a few coins in a tin at home until he has enough for a notebook. In some communities, neighbours save together in a group. Each person puts a small amount into the group every week, and each week one person takes it all.

read.sections.0.simpler.back: Some choices are for today. Some are for later. Spending is using money or things now. Everyone needs to spend on some things, such as food. Saving is setting aside a little money or things for later. Many small amounts become a big amount. Sami puts a few coins into a tin. Not long after, he can buy a notebook. Some neighbours save money in a group. Each person puts in a little money every week. Every week, one person takes all of it.

read.sections.1.text.back: A budget is a plan about how to use money or time. A budget helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. A budget is not only for money. Mei made a time budget for her evening. She planned time to help prepare dinner, rest and read in English for 15 minutes. Making a budget is really about making choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, her time for playing games on the shared phone is reduced by 15 minutes. This is a trade-off (exchange): giving up one thing to get another thing. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you make a choice.
read.sections.1.text.source: A budget is a plan for how to use money or time. It helps you compare what you have with what you need and want. Budgets are not only for money. Mei makes a time budget for her evenings. She plans time to help with dinner, to rest and to read English for 15 minutes. Budgeting is really about choices, and every choice has an opportunity cost. If Mei reads for 15 minutes, she has 15 fewer minutes for games on the shared phone. This is a trade-off: giving up one thing to get another. A careful budget helps you see your trade-offs before you choose.

read.sections.2.text.back: A goal is something you want to do or get, and you work towards it step by step. No one can control everything about the future, and plans can change when the situation around us changes. That is why small and short goals are useful. You can work on these goals now, such as learning 10 new English words a week, practising a skill or taking care of your health. A strong plan is also flexible. Mei's Plan A is to read every night. Plan B, meanwhile, is to read at lunchtime if her evening is busy. A flexible plan still works when life changes.

watch.summary.back: This short video for younger students explains spending and saving. People use money to get things they need and want. But no one can get everything they want. This is called scarcity (shortage), so people have to make choices. Usually, people get what they need first, before what they want. For example, the presenter needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So, lunch comes first. Then, the presenter checks whether there is still money for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But maybe that thing is small, and maybe you have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later, you can get something more expensive. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad of each choice.
watch.summary.source: This short video for younger learners explains spending and saving. People use money to get the things they need and want. But no one can have everything they want. This is called scarcity, so people must make choices. People usually get what they need before what they want. For example, the speaker needs a healthy lunch but wants a cupcake. So lunch comes first. Then the speaker checks if there is money left for the cupcake. When you spend, you get something now. But it may be small, and you may have little money left. When you save, you have to wait, and that can be hard. But later you can get something that costs more. There is no one right answer. Think about the good and bad sides of each choice.

sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson deliberately avoids the topics of salary, bank accounts, loans and long-term career plans. Limit discussion to small, short-term goals that students can control. Do not ask students about where they will live in the future or about their household finances. If a student feels sad when talking about the future, return to the small goals in this lesson and do not push.
